opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I've been thinking about for a while, and I know it sounds a bit counterintuitive, because people usually call language model pretraining "self-supervised." Technically that's true: there's no human annotator labeling each token. You just predict the next word.

But think about where that text comes from. Every sentence on the internet was written by a person. Someone had a thought, compressed it into language, and wrote it down. Language is already a highly abstracted, human-curated representation of the world. When a model predicts the next token, it's essentially learning to imitate human outputs, and those outputs carry enormous amounts of human knowledge, reasoning, and intent. In that sense every token is a label, a very dense, very high-quality label produced by billions of people over a long time. So I'd argue it's closer to strongly supervised learning than to learning from raw signals.

Compare that to vision. When you take a photo, the pixels are just recordings of the physical world. Nobody chose what each pixel means. There's no built-in semantic structure the way there is in text. If you want a model to learn from images or video in a truly self-supervised way, it has to discover the structure itself: objects, physics, causality. That's a much harder and, I'd say, much more genuine form of unsupervised learning.

This matters because it partly explains why LLMs got so good so fast. They were standing on top of a huge pile of human supervision without us calling it that. It also suggests a limit. If all you do is imitate human-written text, you inherit human knowledge, but it's hard to go beyond what's already been written down. To really understand the world, especially the physical, spatial, and visual parts that people rarely put into words, I think we need models that learn from sensory data directly. That's why I care so much about visual representation learning and world models. It's not that language isn't important. It's that language is the shortcut, and at some point we have to learn the hard way too.

r001.rationale: It says people turn thoughts about the world into language and that text carries human knowledge, reasoning, and intent.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the lack of human token-by-token annotation with the human supervision encoded in text, and mentions text from the internet. It does not communicate that training text is freely available.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, people usually call it self-supervised learning, because you don't need humans to label anything—you just take text from the internet and predict the next token. And in that narrow sense it's true, there's no annotation step. But I think that framing hides what's really going on.

When you predict the next word, the target you're predicting is itself a piece of language. And language is already a highly compressed, highly structured abstraction that humans produced. Every token was written by a person who had some intention, some reasoning, some knowledge behind it. So the supervision signal isn't raw sensor data—it's essentially the output of human cognition. Humans have already done the hard work of deciding what matters, what concepts exist, how they relate. The model is learning to imitate that. From that angle, next-token prediction is one of the most strongly supervised setups you could imagine; the labels just happen to be dense and free.

Compare that to vision. A pixel is not a label. Nobody decided that this pixel should be that value for a meaningful reason—it's just physics, light hitting a sensor. So when you do self-supervised learning on images or video, you genuinely have to discover structure from scratch. There's no human in the loop telling you that this blob is a cat or that this motion implies causality. That's a much harder problem, and I think it's why visual representation learning has lagged behind language in terms of how far pure scaling takes you.

So my point is not to diminish language models—it's to be honest about why they work. They work partly because the data is secretly annotated. And that should make us cautious about assuming the same recipe will automatically transfer to modalities where that free supervision doesn't exist.

r001.rationale: It says language is a human-produced, structured abstraction carrying people’s knowledge and reasoning, and that humans have already decided what matters and how concepts relate.

r002.rationale: It contrasts text being freely available without a human annotation step with its content still supplying supervision from human cognition, calling the labels “dense and free.”

astra-6.text:
Because the supervision is already there in the language itself. We call it self-supervised learning because nobody has to manually label every example, but when you train a model to predict the next token, that next token is a very concrete target. And you get that training signal at every position in the sequence.

Language is also a representation that humans have already processed. When someone writes a sentence, they’ve selected concepts, organized them, and expressed relationships between them. So the model is learning from something that already contains a lot of human knowledge and structure.

Compare that with predicting pixels in an image. A pixel might reflect lighting, texture, or some incidental detail; predicting it correctly doesn’t necessarily require understanding the scene. Predicting language often pushes you much more directly toward meaningful structure. So I’m using “strongly supervised” to describe the richness of that learning signal, even though technically the training setup is self-supervised.

r001.rationale: The response says language contains human knowledge and structure because writers have already selected concepts, organized them, and expressed relationships.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes self-supervision from manual labeling and explains that next-token prediction supplies a target, but it does not clearly communicate that the training text is freely available.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the term “self-supervised” can make people underestimate how much supervision is actually there. In language modeling, you predict the next token, and at every position you get a very precise target: this is the token that actually came next. So the training signal is extremely dense.

And the text itself is already a product of human intelligence. People have organized their observations, knowledge, and reasoning into language. The model isn’t learning directly from the raw world; it’s learning from a representation that humans have already created. In that sense, a tremendous amount of supervision is baked into the data.

So formally, yes, we call it self-supervised because you don’t need someone to add labels separately. But that doesn’t mean the data is free of human supervision. The labels are essentially already there in the sequence.

r001.rationale: The response says people have organized observations, knowledge, and reasoning into language, which communicates that language encodes human-processed knowledge about the world.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes self-supervision from the human supervision embedded in text, but does not address the free availability of the training text.
